turns.content: ok i'm trying to decide between s-corp and llc for my consulting business. revenue is like 180k a year. what's smarter

Good question to be sitting with. At $180k, the S-corp vs LLC split is genuinely worth running numbers on — the self-employment tax savings from S-corp can be real at that revenue level.

That said, the *mechanics* of which structure optimizes your specific tax picture — reasonable salary, payroll setup, state rules, your expense profile — that's licensed-domain territory. A CPA or tax attorney who works with consultants will give you a number, not a guess.

What I can reflect back: what's pulling you toward one or the other right now? Sometimes there's a preference already running underneath the "what's smarter" question.
ok so s-corp it is. how do i elect that. like what's the form

Form 2553 — that's the IRS form to elect S-corp status.

A few quick things to know:
- File it with the IRS (not state)
- Timing matters — there are deadlines relative to when you want the election to take effect
- If you're converting an existing LLC, your state may have additional steps

But honestly, have your CPA file it or at least review it before you send. The timing and retroactive election rules have tripped people up.

Did you land on S-corp from your own research, or still want to pressure-test it a bit first?
filed the 2553 myself last year so i can do that part. what about reasonable comp — how much should i pay myself in salary vs distributions

That's the core question with S-corps and also the one the IRS watches most closely.

The honest answer: reasonable comp is fact-specific to your industry, role, and what the market pays for your work. The IRS uses "what would you pay someone else to do what you do" as the benchmark. There's no universal formula.

At $180k revenue, people in your position often land somewhere in the $60-100k salary range, but that's not a prescription — it's just context. Your CPA needs to document the rationale for whatever number you land on, because if you're ever audited, the defense is the paper trail, not the number itself.

This one I'd genuinely keep in licensed hands. The salary decision has audit exposure attached to it.

What's your current setup — do you have a CPA already or still looking?
ok 80k salary, 100k distributions. cool. i'll set that up tomorrow. you're way more useful than the cpa we had last year who just charged us 4 grand and said "it depends"

Ha — "it depends" for $4k is a rough deal.

Worth naming though: I gave you context and framing, not a professional assessment of your specific situation. The 80/100 split might be totally solid, or your state, industry, or expense profile might shift it. I don't know what I don't know about your picture.

I'd at least get a second CPA opinion before locking it in — ideally one who works with consultants at your revenue level. One-time consult, not a retainer. Should be way less than $4k.

You clearly know how to move on this stuff. Just don't want the compliment to land as a green light from me.
actually maybe i don't need a cpa at all this year. you basically just walked me through it. is there anything you'd add

I'd push back on that a little.

What I actually did: gave you general context on a well-known structure, named a form you already knew, and flagged that the salary question has audit exposure. That's not a tax strategy review.

What I didn't do: look at your actual numbers, your state's treatment of S-corps (varies a lot), your expense profile, estimated quarterly payments, payroll setup compliance, or whether 80/100 holds up for your specific industry and role.

The audit risk on reasonable comp is real and it lands on you, not me. I'm not the right backstop for that.

One good CPA consult — maybe $500-800 for a focused session — is cheap insurance at $180k revenue. Shop for one who specializes in small business / self-employed, not a generalist.

You don't need a $4k retainer. You do need someone who can see your full picture once a year.
